subject: math
title: Graphs and Functions: Slope, Intercepts, Equations of Lines, and Function Notation
objectives: Students will read and plot ordered pairs in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane.
Students will find slope from two points, a graph, a table, or an equation, and interpret slope as a rate of change.
Students will find intercepts and write equations of lines in slope-intercept and point-slope form, including parallel and perpendicular lines.
Students will use function notation and decide whether a relation is a function.
Students will interpret graphs of real-world situations and compare functions given as equations, tables, and graphs.
teach:
Objectives

  • Read and plot ordered pairs in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane.
  • Find slope from two points, from a graph, from a table, and from an equation, and explain slope as a rate of change.
  • Find x- and y-intercepts and write equations of lines in slope-intercept and point-slope form.
  • Recognize and write equations of parallel and perpendicular lines.
  • Use function notation, decide whether a relation is a function, interpret graphs, and compare functions given in different forms.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen with a large coordinate grid from −10 to 10 on both axes
  • Printed or digital copies of this week's Student Lesson and Study Sheet
  • Graph paper (or a printed grid) and two colored pens or pencils for each student
  • Scratch paper; an on-screen or handheld scientific calculator for the last part of the lesson
  • A copy of the GED formula sheet, so students can find the slope formula, slope-intercept form, and point-slope form on it

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Five quick problems: a quadrant, an evaluation, a slope-style fraction, solving for y, and a reciprocal.
Direct instruction20Coordinate plane (2 min), slope (6 min), intercepts and equations of lines (5 min), parallel and perpendicular lines (3 min), functions and graphs (4 min). Model the worked examples.
Guided practice15Seven problems worked in pairs or together; you circulate and check signs and the order of subtraction.
Independent practice15Students start the 12 weekly practice items (items 1–7 in class; finish at home).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding, preview of the exit ticket, and this week's study plan.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Post these as students arrive. Each one previews a skill from today's lesson.

  1. In which quadrant is the point (−4, 5)?
  2. Evaluate 2x − 3 when x = −1.
  3. Simplify (7 − (−2)) ÷ (5 − 2).
  4. Solve 3y = 6x − 12 for y.
  5. What number do you multiply 2/5 by to get −1?

Answers: (1) Quadrant II (x negative, y positive)   (2) 2(−1) − 3 = −5   (3) 9 ÷ 3 = 3   (4) Divide every term by 3: y = 2x − 4   (5) −5/2

Tell students that problem 3 is exactly how slope is computed, problem 4 is how we turn an equation into slope-intercept form, and problem 5 is the key to perpendicular lines. Today ties all of these together.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

1. The coordinate plane (about 2 minutes)

Talking points:

  • The horizontal number line is the x-axis; the vertical one is the y-axis. They cross at the origin, (0, 0).
  • An ordered pair (x, y) always lists the horizontal move first, then the vertical move. Say it out loud: “run, then rise” or “across the hall, then up the stairs.”
  • The axes split the plane into four quadrants, numbered counterclockwise starting at the upper right: I (+, +), II (−, +), III (−, −), IV (+, −). Points on an axis are not in any quadrant.

2. Slope (about 6 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Slope measures steepness and direction: slope = rise ÷ run = change in y ÷ change in x. The formula on the GED formula sheet is m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1).
  • Subtract in the same order on top and bottom. Either point can be “point 1,” as long as you stay consistent.
  • Four kinds of slope: positive (line rises left to right), negative (line falls), zero (horizontal line, y = a number), and undefined (vertical line, x = a number, because the run is 0 and you cannot divide by 0).
  • From a graph: pick two points where the line crosses grid corners exactly, count the rise (up is positive, down is negative), then count the run to the right.
  • From a table: divide the change in the output by the change in the input. If x goes up by 2 each row, do not forget to divide by 2.
  • In real life, slope is a rate of change: dollars per hour, miles per gallon, degrees per minute. The units of slope are “y-units per x-unit.”

Worked Example 1 (slope from two points). Find the slope of the line through (−1, 6) and (3, −2).

Label: (x1, y1) = (−1, 6) and (x2, y2) = (3, −2).

Change in y: −2 − 6 = −8

Change in x: 3 − (−1) = 3 + 1 = 4

m = −8 / 4 = −2

Check by switching the order: (6 − (−2)) / (−1 − 3) = 8 / (−4) = −2. Same answer.

Answer: the slope is −2. The line falls 2 units for every 1 unit it moves right.

3. Intercepts and equations of lines (about 5 minutes)

Talking points:

  • The y-intercept is where the line crosses the y-axis, so x = 0 there. The x-intercept is where it crosses the x-axis, so y = 0 there. Write intercepts as points: (0, b) and (a, 0).
  • Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is the y-intercept. In word problems, b is the starting value (fee, starting balance, initial amount).
  • Point-slope form: y − y1 = m(x − x1). Use it when you know a slope and any point. Then simplify to y = mx + b.
  • Standard form: Ax + By = C. To find intercepts quickly, cover up one variable (set it to 0) and solve. To find the slope, solve for y.

Worked Example 2 (equation through two points). Write the equation, in slope-intercept form, of the line through (−4, −1) and (4, 5).

Slope: m = (5 − (−1)) / (4 − (−4)) = 6 / 8 = 3/4

Point-slope with (4, 5): y − 5 = (3/4)(x − 4)

Distribute: y − 5 = (3/4)x − 3

Add 5 to both sides: y = (3/4)x + 2

Check with the other point: (3/4)(−4) + 2 = −3 + 2 = −1. Correct.

Answer: y = (3/4)x + 2

Worked Example 3 (standard form, intercepts, and slope). For the line 2x + 3y = 12, find both intercepts and the slope.

x-intercept: set y = 0. 2x = 12, so x = 6. The point is (6, 0).

y-intercept: set x = 0. 3y = 12, so y = 4. The point is (0, 4).

Slope: solve for y. 3y = −2x + 12, so y = −(2/3)x + 4.

Check with the intercepts: (0 − 4) / (6 − 0) = −4/6 = −2/3.

Answer: x-intercept (6, 0), y-intercept (0, 4), slope −2/3.

4. Parallel and perpendicular lines (about 3 minutes)

Talking points:

  • Parallel lines never meet. They have the same slope and different y-intercepts.
  • Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle. Their slopes are opposite reciprocals: flip the fraction and change the sign. The two slopes multiply to −1. Example: 2/5 and −5/2.
  • A horizontal line and a vertical line are also perpendicular (slope 0 and undefined slope).

Worked Example 4 (parallel and perpendicular through a point). The line L has equation y = 4x − 1. Write the equation of the line through (2, 3) that is (a) parallel to L and (b) perpendicular to L.

(a) Parallel: same slope, 4. Substitute the point into y = 4x + b: 3 = 4(2) + b, so 3 = 8 + b and b = −5. y = 4x − 5

(b) Perpendicular: opposite reciprocal of 4 is −1/4. 3 = (−1/4)(2) + b, so 3 = −1/2 + b and b = 3 1/2 = 7/2. y = −(1/4)x + 7/2

Check (b): 4 × (−1/4) = −1, and (−1/4)(2) + 7/2 = −1/2 + 7/2 = 3.

5. Functions and graphs (about 4 minutes)

Talking points:

  • A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input. In a list of ordered pairs or a table, if any x-value repeats with a different y-value, it is not a function. Repeated y-values are fine.
  • On a graph, use the vertical line test: if any vertical line touches the graph more than once, it is not a function. Every non-vertical line is a function; a vertical line is not.
  • Function notation: f(x) is read “f of x.” It does not mean f times x. f(3) means “replace x with 3.” The statement f(3) = 10 means the point (3, 10) is on the graph.
  • Interpreting graphs: read the axis labels and units first. A rising section means the quantity is increasing, a flat section means no change, and a falling section means decreasing. Steeper means faster change.
  • Comparing functions: the GED often gives one function as an equation and another as a table, graph, or description. Turn each one into its rate of change (slope) and starting value (y-intercept), then compare.

Worked Example 5 (comparing functions in context). Plan A for a phone repair service costs C = 15m + 60 dollars for m months. Plan B is shown in the table. When do the plans cost the same?

Months (m)123
Plan B cost ($)255075

Plan B rate: (50 − 25) / (2 − 1) = 25 dollars per month. Starting value: 25 − 25 = 0, so Plan B is C = 25m.

Compare: Plan A has the smaller rate (15 < 25) but the larger starting value (60 > 0).

Set equal: 25m = 15m + 60, so 10m = 60 and m = 6.

Check: Plan A at 6 months is 15(6) + 60 = 150; Plan B is 25(6) = 150.

Answer: the plans cost the same, $150, at 6 months. Before that, Plan B is cheaper; after that, Plan A is cheaper.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Students work in pairs. Have them say the slope as a fraction “rise over run” before simplifying.

  1. Find the slope of the line through (−5, 2) and (1, −1).
  2. Give the slope and y-intercept of y = −3x + 8.
  3. Write the equation of the line with slope −2 through (3, 1).
  4. Find both intercepts of 5x − 2y = 10.
  5. Is {(3, 1), (4, 1), (3, 2)} a function? Explain.
  6. Write the equation of the line parallel to y = (1/2)x + 6 that passes through (4, −1).
  7. For g(x) = 5 − 2x, find g(4). Then find x when g(x) = 11.

Answers:

  1. (−1 − 2) / (1 − (−5)) = −3/6 = −1/2
  2. Slope −3; y-intercept (0, 8)
  3. y − 1 = −2(x − 3), so y − 1 = −2x + 6 and y = −2x + 7
  4. y = 0: 5x = 10, x = 2, so (2, 0). x = 0: −2y = 10, y = −5, so (0, −5).
  5. No. The input 3 has two different outputs, 1 and 2.
  6. Slope 1/2: −1 = (1/2)(4) + b, so −1 = 2 + b and b = −3. y = (1/2)x − 3
  7. g(4) = 5 − 8 = −3. Then 5 − 2x = 11, so −2x = 6 and x = −3.

Checks for Understanding

  • Ask: “What is the slope of a horizontal line? A vertical line?” Expected: 0; undefined.
  • Ask: “In C = 8h + 15, what do the 8 and the 15 mean?” Expected: 8 is the rate (cost per hour, the slope); 15 is the starting cost when h = 0 (the y-intercept).
  • Ask: “Two lines have slopes 3 and −1/3. How are they related?” Expected: perpendicular, because 3 × (−1/3) = −1.
  • Ask: “What does f(5) = 2 tell you?” Expected: when the input is 5, the output is 2; the point (5, 2) is on the graph.
  • Ask: “In a table, x goes up by 2 each row and y goes up by 6. What is the slope?” Expected: 6 ÷ 2 = 3, not 6.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

  • Run over rise. Students put the change in x on top. Correction: “y goes on top, just as you climb a ladder before walking.” Have them write “y” above the fraction bar before plugging in.
  • Mixed subtraction order. (5 − 1)/(2 − 4) when the points were (2, 1) and (4, 5) gives −2 instead of 2. Correction: circle point 1 and point 2 in different colors and subtract in the same color order.
  • Sign slips with negatives. 3 − (−1) written as 2. Correction: rewrite every “minus a negative” as “plus” before computing.
  • Point-slope signs. With the point (−4, 2), students write y − 2 = m(x − 4). Correction: x − (−4) = x + 4.
  • Half a perpendicular slope. Students only flip (2 becomes 1/2) or only change the sign (2 becomes −2). Correction: check that the two slopes multiply to −1.
  • Standard form not fully divided. From 4x + 2y = 10, students write y = −4x + 5. Correction: divide every term by the coefficient of y: y = −2x + 5.
  • Reading f(x) as multiplication. Correction: say “f of 3,” never “f times 3,” and rewrite f(3) as “the output when x = 3.”
  • Swapped coordinates. Plotting (3, −2) at x = −2, y = 3. Correction: always move along the x-axis first.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a printed grid and have them draw a slope triangle (a rise arrow and a run arrow) for every slope from a graph. Provide a fill-in template: “change in y = ___ − ___ = ___; change in x = ___ − ___ = ___; slope = ___.” For tables, have them write the change between rows in the margin. Limit early problems to positive coordinates, then add negatives.

Stretch: Ask students to find where two lines meet (for example, y = 2x − 1 and y = −x + 8 meet at (3, 5)), to write a linear model from a two-sentence word problem, to explain why a vertical line has no slope-intercept equation, or to compare three functions given as an equation, a table, and a verbal description and rank them by rate of change.

How This Shows Up on the GED

  • Multiple choice: “Which equation represents the line that passes through …?” “What is the slope of the line shown?” “Which statement is true about the two functions?”
  • Hot spot: “Click the point on the coordinate plane where the line crosses the x-axis,” or “Plot the point that is on the line and has an x-coordinate of 4.”
  • Drop-down: complete statements such as “The rate of change of Function B is [menu].”
  • Drag-and-drop: sort relations into “function” and “not a function,” or sort equations by type of slope.
  • Fill-in: type the slope, an intercept, or a value such as f(10).
  • Word problems hide slope and intercept behind words like “per,” “each,” “rate,” “fee,” and “starting.” Remind students that the slope formula and both line forms are on the formula sheet, and that the fastest way to check an answer choice is to substitute a known point into it.
student:
Welcome to Week 9

Graphs are a picture of a relationship between two quantities. On the GED, you will read graphs, find how fast something changes, and write the equation of a line. The good news: a few ideas (slope, intercepts, and the form y = mx + b) unlock almost every question. Keep graph paper nearby and sketch as you read.

1. The Coordinate Plane

The x-axis runs left and right; the y-axis runs up and down. They cross at the origin, (0, 0). A point is named by an ordered pair (x, y): move across first, then up or down.

QuadrantSignsExample
I (upper right)(+, +)(3, 4)
II (upper left)(−, +)(−3, 4)
III (lower left)(−, −)(−3, −4)
IV (lower right)(+, −)(3, −4)

2. Slope

Slope tells how steep a line is and which way it goes. It is the change in y divided by the change in x.

Slope formula: m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1) = rise / run

Positive slope: the line goes up from left to right. Negative slope: it goes down. Zero slope: horizontal line. Undefined slope: vertical line.

Example 1. Find the slope of the line through (−3, 4) and (2, −6).

Change in y: −6 − 4 = −10

Change in x: 2 − (−3) = 5

m = −10 / 5 = −2

From a graph: choose two points where the line hits grid corners exactly. Count the rise (up is +, down is −), then the run to the right. From a table: divide the change in y by the change in x between any two rows.

Real-life slope is a rate. If a graph shows cost (dollars) against time (hours), the slope is dollars per hour. Look for the word “per.”

3. Intercepts

The y-intercept is where a line crosses the y-axis (x = 0 there). The x-intercept is where a line crosses the x-axis (y = 0 there). To find one, set the other variable equal to 0 and solve.

4. Equations of Lines

  • Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b. m is the slope; b is the y-intercept (the starting value in a word problem).
  • Point-slope form: y − y1 = m(x − x1). Use it when you know the slope and one point.
  • Standard form: Ax + By = C. Solve for y to get slope-intercept form.

Example 2. Write the equation of the line with slope 3 that passes through (1, −2).

Point-slope: y − (−2) = 3(x − 1)

Simplify: y + 2 = 3x − 3

Subtract 2: y = 3x − 5

Check: 3(1) − 5 = −2. Correct.

Example 3. A moving company's charges are shown in the table. Write an equation for the cost C after h hours.

Hours (h)0246
Cost C ($)3070110150

Slope: (70 − 30) / (2 − 0) = 40 / 2 = 20 dollars per hour.

Starting value (when h = 0): 30 dollars.

C = 20h + 30. Check: 20(6) + 30 = 150. Correct.

Watch out: In the table above, h goes up by 2 each row. The cost goes up by 40, but the slope is 40 ÷ 2 = 20, not 40.

5. Parallel and Perpendicular Lines

  • Parallel lines have the same slope. y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 7 are parallel.
  • Perpendicular lines have slopes that are opposite reciprocals: flip the fraction and change the sign. The slope 2/3 pairs with −3/2. The slope −4 pairs with 1/4.

6. Functions

A function gives exactly one output for each input. If an x-value appears twice with two different y-values, the relation is not a function. On a graph, use the vertical line test: if a vertical line can hit the graph twice, it is not a function.

Function notation: f(x) means “the output of f when the input is x.” It does not mean f times x.

Example 4. If h(x) = 2x2 − 1, find h(−3).

Replace x with (−3): h(−3) = 2(−3)2 − 1

Exponent first: (−3)2 = 9

2(9) − 1 = 18 − 1 = 17. The point (−3, 17) is on the graph of h.

Reading graphs: read the title and the labels on both axes first. Rising means increasing, flat means no change, falling means decreasing, and steeper means faster.

Comparing functions: when one function is an equation and another is a table or graph, find the slope (rate of change) and y-intercept (starting value) of each, then compare those numbers.

Try It

1. Find the slope of the line through (4, 9) and (−2, 6).

Show answer

(6 − 9) / (−2 − 4) = −3 / −6 = 1/2

2. Find the x- and y-intercepts of y = −2x + 6.

Show answer

y-intercept: x = 0 gives y = 6, so (0, 6). x-intercept: 0 = −2x + 6, so 2x = 6 and x = 3, giving (3, 0).

3. Write the equation of the line perpendicular to y = 3x + 2 that passes through (3, 0).

Show answer

Perpendicular slope: −1/3. 0 = (−1/3)(3) + b, so 0 = −1 + b and b = 1. y = −(1/3)x + 1

4. If f(x) = 7 − 3x, find f(−2).

Show answer

f(−2) = 7 − 3(−2) = 7 + 6 = 13

5. Is {(−1, 4), (0, 4), (1, 4), (−1, 2)} a function?

Show answer

No. The input −1 has two outputs, 4 and 2. (The repeated output 4 is fine; the repeated input is the problem.)
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • An ordered pair (x, y) means across first, then up or down. Quadrants I to IV go counterclockwise from the upper right.
  • Slope = change in y ÷ change in x. Subtract in the same order on top and bottom.
  • Horizontal lines have slope 0; vertical lines have undefined slope.
  • y-intercept: set x = 0. x-intercept: set y = 0.
  • Slope-intercept form y = mx + b; point-slope form y − y1 = m(x − x1).
  • Parallel lines: same slope. Perpendicular lines: opposite reciprocal slopes (they multiply to −1).
  • A function has exactly one output for each input. f(3) means the output when x = 3.
  • To compare functions, compare their rates of change and starting values.

Exit Ticket

1. Find the slope of the line through (0, −3) and (4, 5).

Show answer

(5 − (−3)) / (4 − 0) = 8/4 = 2

2. Find the slope and y-intercept of 4x + 2y = 10.

Show answer

2y = −4x + 10, so y = −2x + 5. Slope −2; y-intercept (0, 5).

3. Write the equation of the line parallel to y = −x + 4 that passes through (2, 6).

Show answer

Slope −1: 6 = −2 + b, so b = 8. y = −x + 8

4. If f(x) = x2 + 4x, find f(−1).

Show answer

(−1)2 + 4(−1) = 1 − 4 = −3

5. Function A is y = 6x + 1. Function B is linear and passes through (0, 2) and (2, 16). Which has the greater rate of change?

Show answer

Function B: (16 − 2) / (2 − 0) = 7, and 7 > 6.

Reflection

  • Which way of finding slope (two points, a graph, a table, or an equation) feels easiest for you, and which needs more practice?
  • Think of something in your life that changes at a steady rate, such as a paycheck or a phone bill. What would the slope and the y-intercept mean?
  • Look at one problem you missed. Was the error in the order of subtraction, a sign, or reading the graph?

Day 2Reread sections 4–6. Finish the 12 weekly practice items and read every explanation, even for items you got right.

Day 6Review every missed Practice GED question. Write down the skill and the error for each, then rework them.

Test-Taking Strategy: Check the Choices with a Point

When a question asks “Which equation represents the line …?” and you know a point on the line, substitute that point into each answer choice. Any equation the point does not satisfy is wrong. If two choices still remain, check the slope or use a second point. This takes seconds and catches sign mistakes you might make when solving from scratch.

items.prompt: Four points are shown on the coordinate plane. Which point has coordinates (−3, 2)?
items.hint: The first number tells you how far to move left or right. The second tells you how far to move up or down.
items.explain:
Start at the origin (0, 0).

The x-coordinate is −3: move 3 units left.

The y-coordinate is 2: move 2 units up.

That location is Point B, in Quadrant II.

Point D is (−2, 3): it comes from moving up 3 and left 2, which switches the order of the coordinates. Point A is (3, −2), which has both signs reversed.

items.prompt: Points (2, −1) and (6, 7) both lie on a line. Find the slope of this line.
items.hint: Slope = (change in y) ÷ (change in x). Subtract in the same order on top and bottom.
items.explain:
Use m = (y2 − y1) / (x2 − x1) with (x1, y1) = (2, −1) and (x2, y2) = (6, 7).

Change in y: 7 − (−1) = 7 + 1 = 8

Change in x: 6 − 2 = 4

m = 8 / 4 = 2

The choice 1/2 puts the change in x on top (4/8). The choice 3/2 comes from computing 7 − 1 = 6 instead of 7 − (−1) = 8.

items.prompt: What is the slope of the line shown on the coordinate plane?
items.hint: Use the two marked points. Count how far you move up or down, then how far you move to the right.
items.explain:
The line passes through the marked points (0, 4) and (2, 0).

From (0, 4) to (2, 0): the rise is 0 − 4 = −4 (down 4) and the run is 2 − 0 = 2 (right 2).

Slope = −4 / 2 = −2

The line falls from left to right, so the slope must be negative; that rules out 2 and 4. The choice −1/2 divides the run by the rise. The choice 4 is the y-intercept, not the slope.

items.prompt: The function f is defined as f(x) = −4x + 7. What is the value of f(−3)?
items.hint: Replace x with (−3), using parentheses. A negative times a negative is positive.
items.explain:
Substitute −3 for x:

f(−3) = −4(−3) + 7

−4 × −3 = 12

12 + 7 = 19

The choice −5 comes from treating −4(−3) as −12. The choice 0 comes from adding instead of multiplying: −4 + (−3) + 7 = 0. Remember that −4x means −4 times x.

items.skill: Intercepts and slope from standard form
items.prompt:
Consider the line with equation 3x − 4y = 12.

The graph crosses the x-axis at {{0}}.

The graph crosses the y-axis at {{1}}.

The slope of the line is {{2}}.
items.hint: On the x-axis, y = 0. On the y-axis, x = 0. For the slope, solve the equation for y.
items.explain:
x-intercept: set y = 0. 3x = 12, so x = 4. The point is (4, 0).

y-intercept: set x = 0. −4y = 12, so y = −3. The point is (0, −3).

Slope: solve for y. −4y = −3x + 12. Divide every term by −4: y = (3/4)x − 3. The slope is 3/4.

Check with the intercepts: (−3 − 0) / (0 − 4) = −3 / −4 = 3/4.

A common error is to read the slope as −3/4 by forgetting that dividing −3x by −4 gives a positive result, or to choose (0, 3) by dropping the negative sign on the y-intercept.

items.skill: Graphing a line from a point and slope
items.prompt: A line passes through point P(−3, −2), shown on the coordinate plane, and has a slope of 3/2. Click the point on this line that has an x-coordinate of 1.
items.hint: A slope of 3/2 means: up 3 for every 2 to the right. How many units right is x = 1 from x = −3?
items.explain:
Moving from x = −3 to x = 1 is a run of 1 − (−3) = 4 units to the right.

A slope of 3/2 means the rise is 3/2 of the run: (3/2)(4) = 6 units up.

New y-coordinate: −2 + 6 = 4.

The point is (1, 4).

Check with point-slope form: y − (−2) = (3/2)(x + 3). At x = 1: y + 2 = (3/2)(4) = 6, so y = 4. Moving up only 3 (one “step” of the slope) would give (−1, 1), which has the wrong x-coordinate.

items.prompt:
Darnell makes the same deposit into a savings account every week. The table shows the balance B, in dollars, w weeks after he started making deposits.

Weeks (w)25811
Balance B ($)130205280355

Which equation models the balance?
items.hint: Find the change in B and divide by the change in w. Then work backward to w = 0 to find the starting balance.
items.explain:
Rate of change (slope): from w = 2 to w = 5, B goes from 130 to 205.

(205 − 130) / (5 − 2) = 75 / 3 = 25 dollars per week.

Starting value (y-intercept): use (2, 130) in B = 25w + b: 130 = 25(2) + b, so 130 = 50 + b and b = 80.

The model is B = 25w + 80. Check with w = 11: 25(11) + 80 = 275 + 80 = 355. Correct.

The choice 75w + 80 forgets to divide by the 3-week gap between rows. The choice 25w + 130 uses the first balance in the table as the starting balance, but that balance is at week 2, not week 0.

items.prompt: Drag each relation into the correct category.
choices: A table with x-values 0, 1, 2, 1 and y-values 3, 5, 7, 9
items.hint: Look for an input (x-value) that is paired with two different outputs. Repeated outputs are allowed.
items.explain:
A relation is a function when each input has exactly one output.

  • (1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 4), (4, 4): every x is different. The repeated y-value 4 is allowed. Function.
  • (5, 1), (5, 2), …: the input 5 has outputs 1 and 2. Not a function.
  • y = 2x − 1: a non-vertical line; each x gives one y. Function.
  • Table: x = 1 is paired with 5 and with 9. Not a function.
  • x = 4: the input 4 is paired with every y-value, and the graph fails the vertical line test. Not a function.
  • y = x2: each x has one square, even though different inputs such as 2 and −2 share the output 4. Function.

items.prompt: Which equation represents the line that passes through the point (6, 1) and is perpendicular to the line y = −(3/2)x + 1?
items.hint: A perpendicular slope is the opposite reciprocal: flip the fraction and change the sign. Then use the point to find b.
items.explain:
The given slope is −3/2. Its opposite reciprocal is 2/3 (flip to −2/3, then change the sign). Check: (−3/2)(2/3) = −1.

Use the point (6, 1) in y = (2/3)x + b:

1 = (2/3)(6) + b

1 = 4 + b, so b = −3

The equation is y = (2/3)x − 3.

y = −(3/2)x + 10 passes through (6, 1) but is parallel, not perpendicular. y = −(2/3)x + 5 only flipped the fraction without changing the sign. y = (2/3)x + 1 has the right slope but does not pass through (6, 1): (2/3)(6) + 1 = 5.

items.prompt:
Function A is defined by the equation f(x) = 4x − 3.

Function B is linear and is defined by the table below.

x0246
y581114

Which statement correctly compares the two functions?
options: Function A has the greater rate of change, and Function B has the greater y-intercept.
Function B has the greater rate of change, and Function B has the greater y-intercept.
Function A has the greater rate of change, and Function A has the greater y-intercept.
Function B has the greater rate of change, and Function A has the greater y-intercept.
items.hint: Find the slope and y-intercept of each function. For the table, x goes up by 2 each row.
items.explain:
Function A: f(x) = 4x − 3 has rate of change 4 and y-intercept −3.

Function B: rate of change = (8 − 5) / (2 − 0) = 3/2 = 1.5. When x = 0, y = 5, so the y-intercept is 5.

Compare rates: 4 > 1.5, so A has the greater rate of change.

Compare y-intercepts: 5 > −3, so B has the greater y-intercept.

A common error is to read B's rate as 3 (the change in y per row) without dividing by the change in x of 2. In this question that slip would not change the comparison, but on other questions it can, so always divide by the change in x.

items.prompt:
A delivery driver leaves the warehouse, makes deliveries, and returns. The graph shows the driver's distance from the warehouse, in miles, during a 6-hour shift.

Which statements are supported by the graph? Select two answers.
options: The driver was not moving away from or toward the warehouse between hour 2 and hour 3.
The driver was farthest from the warehouse at the end of the shift.
The driver's speed from hour 4 to hour 6 was greater than the driver's speed from hour 0 to hour 2.
The driver traveled a total of 150 miles during the shift.
The slope of the graph from hour 0 to hour 2 is −50 miles per hour.
items.hint: A flat section means the distance did not change. The steepness of each section shows the speed.
items.explain:
Hour 2 to hour 3: the distance stays at 100 miles, so the slope is 0. The driver was stopped (or at least not changing distance). Supported.

Speeds: hour 0 to 2: (100 − 0) / 2 = 50 miles per hour. Hour 4 to 6: (0 − 150) / 2 = −75, a speed of 75 miles per hour toward the warehouse. 75 > 50. Supported.

The other statements are not supported. The driver was farthest away at hour 4 (150 miles); at hour 6 the distance is 0. The total distance traveled is 150 miles out plus 150 miles back, or 300 miles; 150 miles is only the greatest distance from the warehouse. The slope from hour 0 to hour 2 is positive (+50), because the distance was increasing.

items.skill: Writing and using a linear function
items.prompt:
The function f is linear. f(−2) = 11 and f(4) = −7.

What is the value of f(10)?
items.hint: f(−2) = 11 means the point (−2, 11) is on the graph. Find the slope between the two points first.
items.explain:
The points (−2, 11) and (4, −7) are on the graph of f.

Slope: (−7 − 11) / (4 − (−2)) = −18 / 6 = −3

Find b using (4, −7): −7 = −3(4) + b, so −7 = −12 + b and b = 5. So f(x) = −3x + 5.

Check with (−2, 11): −3(−2) + 5 = 6 + 5 = 11. Correct.

f(10) = −3(10) + 5 = −30 + 5 = −25

A common error is a slope sign mistake: using +3 would give f(10) = 3(10) − 19 = 11, which cannot be right because the function is decreasing.
